title: Electoral Reforms

cards.b: India holds the world's largest elections, yet money, muscle, caste and misinformation distort them. Electoral reform is one of the most repeated topics in GS and PSIR. Know the committees, the Supreme Court rulings and the live proposals such as simultaneous polls.

• Art. 324-329: Election Commission and elections.
  • RPA 1950: rolls, seats. RPA 1951: conduct, disqualification, corrupt practices.
  • Model Code of Conduct (convention, no statutory force).
  • Tenth Schedule: defection. 61st Amendment (1988): voting age 18.

The system is first-past-the-post (FPTP): simple, but winners can have under 50 per cent votes, and seats and votes can diverge.
Later: NCRWC (2002), Second ARC (2007), Law Commission 255th Report (2015).

ADR v Union of India (2002) and PUCL v Union of India (2003): voters have a right to know criminal, financial and educational backgrounds of candidates, via affidavits (Art. 19(1)(a)). Lily Thomas (2013): a legislator convicted with two or more years' jail is disqualified at once. The Court has asked parties to publish candidates' criminal records and reasons for selecting them. Fast-track courts for MP-MLA cases (Ashwini Upadhyay, 2016 onward).

Spending ceilings apply to candidates but not parties. The Electoral Bonds scheme (2018) allowed anonymous donations through banks. In ADR v Union of India (15 February 2024) a five-judge Bench unanimously struck it down as violating the voter's right to information (Art. 19(1)(a)) and ordered disclosure. Proposals: state funding in part (Indrajit Gupta), a National Election Fund, audit of party accounts, and tax-based transparency.

• NOTA (PUCL, 2013), a right to negative vote, with no electoral effect.
  • EVMs and VVPAT: in April 2024 the Court rejected a demand for 100 per cent VVPAT counting.
  • EC appointments: Anoop Baranwal (2023) set a panel of PM, Leader of Opposition and CJI; the 2023 Act replaced the CJI with a Union minister, and this is contested.
  • Voter rolls: the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) began in Bihar in 2025 and spread to 12 states and UTs from late 2025. The Court allowed it, and critics fear exclusion of genuine voters. Check the latest.

• One Nation, One Election: the 129th Constitution Amendment Bill and a UT-laws bill were introduced in December 2024 and sent to a Joint Parliamentary Committee, whose term was extended in 2026. Arguments: lower cost, steady governance. Against: federalism, and shortening of state-assembly terms (as of 2026 under study).
  • Women's reservation: the 106th Amendment (2023) gives 33 per cent in Lok Sabha and assemblies, effective after the Census and delimitation.
  • Proportional or mixed systems; ranked voting; ban on candidates contesting two seats.

Supporters: disclosure and NOTA gave voters tools. Critics: the Model Code is toothless; criminals still win; money grows; the EC is seen as less independent; digital misinformation, deepfakes and paid news are new threats. Think of reform as four fronts: candidates, parties, the EC and the voters.

Compare with the UK (state limits on party spending), Germany (mixed-member proportional), and Brazil (compulsory voting). A sensible package: independent EC appointments, internal party democracy, transparent funding, swift trial of election offences, and voter education.
